### Step Analysis:
This step correctly sets up the proof by stating the hypothesis of the theorem: that \((x_n)\) converges to some limit \(L\). The student then writes the definition of convergence with \(\varepsilon/2\) instead of \(\varepsilon\). This is a valid and common technique in analysis proofs, as choosing \(\varepsilon/2\) at the start will simplify later inequalities when proving the Cauchy condition. The logical structure is sound: from the assumption of convergence, we can apply the definition with any positive \(\varepsilon\), and here \(\varepsilon/2 > 0\) since \(\varepsilon > 0\). No logical errors are present in this step.

### Mathematical Review:
The definition of convergence is: \(∀ \varepsilon > 0, ∃ N ∈ ℕ \text{ such that } ∀ n ≥ N, |x_n - L| < \varepsilon\).  
The student wrote: "For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), ∃ \(N ∈ ℕ\) such that ∀ \(n ≥ N\), \(|x_n - L| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\)."  
This is equivalent to the standard definition because if \(\varepsilon > 0\), then \(\varepsilon/2 > 0\), and the definition holds for that positive number. Formally, given \(\varepsilon > 0\), apply the definition of convergence with \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/2 > 0\) to get an \(N\) such that \(|x_n - L| < \varepsilon/2\) ∀ \(n ≥ N\). The notation and quantifiers are correctly used.

None. The step is mathematically precise and logically valid.
